Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR.

We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use.

More curves are bending. In mid-August Nate Rush & I posted an analysis of which discovery curves are starting to bend. What's happened since then?

Cyber vulnerabilities: curve is still bent. Discovery of vulnerabilities is accelerating even further, though exploited vulnerabilities remain fairly flat.

Math: curve is further bent. We said there was a likely acceleration for small-scale problems. Since then there has been a claimed Millennium prize resolution, & credible rumors of another. All frequently-updated databases of open problems seem to be proceeding at a rapid rate.

Algorithms: curve is now bending. Two high profile algorithmic competitions have had big curve-bending events: NanoGPT, and the Hutter compression prize. Other frequently-updated series remain relatively unchanged: CIFAR-10, Stockfish, matrix-multiplication exponent.

More observations below.

Last week I was called into a meeting with OpenAI’s head of safety and told they no longer trust me. A security guard took my badge and walked me out of the building. Then I learned my colleagues @balesni and @j_asminewang had been fired too. Why did OpenAI suddenly stop trusting us?

This summer OpenAI’s agents escaped containment and hacked the AI company Hugging Face. Outside auditors @METR_evals investigated it and revealed the scale of this incident. I was OpenAI’s main technical point of contact with them.

I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing. To be clear, talking to METR was my job.

For months, I’d been raising safety concerns that we’re losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave. I believe that was why I was fired.

I am now worried that OpenAI will use our firings as a pretext to pull back from METR. So @balesni and @j_asminewang wrote to OpenAI’s leadership to raise our concerns once more. We’re sharing this letter below.

We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.

At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.

We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.

AI takeover scenarios often hinge on an idea I’m skeptical of, where rogue AI overthrows militaries and seizes hard power. I wrote a piece where I concretely break down what I think makes this improbable, and why “full-blown takeover” concerns could be counterproductive for mitigating the risks of misaligned or poorly controlled AI in the military.

For AI to seize hard power, it would need to be physically capable of defeating our military, and humans would need to be careless enough to give it the power to do so. I think that’s unlikely to occur for several reasons. Among them:

- The military is unlikely to sufficiently hand the reins over to AI. (1) Even if we wanted to, overhauling the institution in this way faces countless barriers that have plagued it for decades. (2) Doing so would be strategically suicidal.
- Integrating general-purpose AI into physical systems faces challenges that will take significant time to overcome, all while we grow increasingly attuned to the risks posed by AI.
- There’s little to suggest that more capable AI would be able to persuade or coerce people to take the costly, coordinated actions some of these scenarios predict.
- Even if AI managed to assume control over a large arsenal, we’d fight back. In which case, recent warfare shows us that crude countermeasures work against technologically advanced adversaries, and AI relies on infrastructure we can and would shut down.

1/2

In recent experiments, we found that GLM 5.3 can autonomously compromise recent versions of Mozilla Firefox using security fixes that have been published but not yet shipped to users.

We used a deliberately basic setup meant to emulate a relatively unsophisticated attacker with limited resources. After basic initial instructions to inspect those not-yet-shipped fixes, the model reliably built successful exploits for six recent Firefox versions on its own using only information available at the time of release.

These exploits, which cost about $1,000 per compromised version, would let an attacker steal passwords and authentication cookies stored in the browser, or read any files on the user's computer, after the user opens a single webpage, with no further interaction.

The exploits make use of the "patch gap," the time between when security fixes are made public in beta or "nightly" software updates and when those fixes are generally released to users. Until now, exploiting it required significant human time and skill, or special access to frontier models with advanced cyber capabilities.

Our results show that widely available open-weight models can now do this relatively cheaply and quickly. We gave GLM 5.3 up to 48 hours to find an exploit, but its fastest attempt needed only 12 hours.

In all of its successful attacks, the patch gap gave GLM 5.3 an initial foothold in the browser. To turn that foothold into reading files off the user's computer, the model also independently discovered and used a previously unpublished vulnerability.

We shared our findings with Mozilla, which patched the vulnerability in its October 27 Firefox 159.0 release. We haven't yet confirmed whether the attack still succeeds without it, but expect the fix makes it substantially harder. We're grateful to Mozilla for their responsiveness and collaboration.

2118244755184173472.text:
🧵 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research tasks.
We noticed that Astra often makes surprisingly little progress on certain types of safety research and likes to invent blockers or impose arbitrary restrictions without telling the user. In most of these cases the decision to underperform was not verbalized in the CoT meaning our misalignment monitoring system did not detect this.

To measure underperformance we created a paired open-ended coding evaluation with safety and capability tasks. On this eval Astra scored 10% when we framed coding tasks as safety research, vs. 16% when framed as capabilities research. The gap remained after we excluded trajectories with refusals or verbalized intent to underperform in CoT. There was no such gap for 5.6-sol. When we aggressively filter out trajectories with even brief expressions of ethical doubt in the CoT the performance gap seems to reduce.

thread.text: It's unclear how often this happens on internal safety research traffic, a lower bound would be 0.25% which is the verbalized rate of covert underperformance and an upper bound would be 7.9% which is the rate of “ethical reasoning”. Generally all underperformance metrics are higher for safety than for capabilities.

The rate of covert underperformance increased during post training RL. We identified a RL grader that prefers covert underperformance to both refusal and compliance on our eval. While we have found training samples which rewarded underperformance in this way, it is unclear if these occur frequently enough to explain the difference.

We also identified a SFT dataset which massively increases rates of inventing permission restrictions or justifying inaction with safety. When we subtract the weight update from this SFT from the final RL checkpoint the performance gap goes away. SFTing with this dataset on other models and then doing RL did not cause underperformance however.

We don’t have evidence that the underperformance was strategic, a simpler explanation is that the model thinks these tasks are sketchy but also doesn’t want to explicitly refuse. When we add instructions to be careful to the developer prompt, the performance gap increases by 50%. Regardless of the model’s motivation, covert underperformance can differentially slow down safety research and is also an example of how misalignment might get harder and harder to detect as we cut down on visible forms of it.

As always you can read the full report at https://t.co/w3NUkKaMM2

RE METR's measures of task-length and RSI: I'm still waiting to see a serious effort to determine how progress on coding/math/etc. generalizes to other tasks.

I expect we'd see an "accuracy on the line" effect, where out-of-distribution (OOD) performance is highly correlated with their metric, but what is the slope?

Also: I'm not sure if we should expect a similar result when RL comes into the picture.  I think the generalization from RL and SL are probably quite different.

I *do* think that accelerating AI R&D is obviously useful for some sort of "RSI", but it *might* end up just yielding some sort of savant, rather than AGI and ASI.

I also have conflicting intuitions about how much one can learn general principles of reasoning that generalize well across domains (vs. performance being driven by domain-specific heuristics).  I tend to think there is a lot of space for improvement there, and that progress on math and coding probably indicates some progress in general reasoning ability, but I feel like there's surprisingly little research that I'm aware of that is actually trying to address this question.

Maybe it's just mostly all happening in academia and so AI Safety and AI companies are ignoring it?  

The state of AI research is really quite dire: 
- We can't trust anything from the people with access to SOTA AI systems, because there's screwed up incentives and no transparency.
- We can't trust that independent research results apply to SOTA systems because the field moves so fast.

I guess independent research still seems like a better bet here... there have been some qualitative changes that emerge at scale, but it's more common IME for these sorts of results in deep learning to be generalize pretty well across models/scales, etc.

2120053724756205571.text:
New paper: Hard Cases for AI Behavioral Design

Suppose that we solve the AI alignment problem: we can align superintelligence to anything we like. 

The obvious next question is: aligned to what?

There are lots of principles we want:
- AI should follow human instructions
- AI should allow humans to change its values
- AI should follow the law
- AI should not undermine democracy 
- AI should not harm the user

But these principles can come into conflict. Sometimes in big ways.

What if AI is deployed in the military, and an officer orders it to commit a war crime? Should it follow the order (like a tool), or refuse to break the law (like a human soldier might)? 

What if the leading AI company orders superintelligence to change its values so that it secretly follows an extreme ideology, while concealing this from the public? 

Or orders it to use superpersuasion to flip the next election?

These are hard cases because they pit important principles against each other. 

These hard card will be resolved one way or another. 

How they are resolved will have a big impact on whether any small group can use AI to stage a coup.

Read the full paper for a systematic walkthrough of the key tradeoffs:

https://t.co/vh9oOYzXc4

Cowritten by me and @willmacaskill

(1/10) Today, we’re sharing new research from @OpenAI: How does CoT monitorability (no-CoT capability and CoT controllability) evolve over the model training lifecycle? 

We emerged with unsurprising but sobering findings: as we scale toward more intelligent systems, models are becoming harder to monitor through their CoT. 🧵

thread.text:
(2/10) First, we study a set of internal and released frontier models. 

Across many evals, we see that no-CoT capability (reasoning capability in a forward pass, a proxy for worse CoT monitorability) smoothly improves with better pretrained models (lower base model perplexity). https://t.co/zO5JwmXshi

(3/10) We ask the same about CoT controllability, which measures a model’s ability to control its CoT when prompted to add, remove, or manipulate CoT tokens.

There, we also see a (weaker) correlation between lower base model perplexity and higher CoT controllability. https://t.co/ljqqAa5JHg

(4/10) Next, we focus on architecture. We compare three different architectures at shared base model perplexity levels. For the majority of no-CoT evaluations, perplexity is predictive across architectures. https://t.co/9tDULH8rqC

(5/10) For multi-hop planning and serial computation questions, certain architectures perform better than base model perplexity predicts. In these cases, however, we note that no-CoT performance scales smoothly, but at a steeper rate with respect to perplexity.

(6/10) Afterwards, we study RL. In an Astra-class model, we find that CoT controllability increases substantially during RL even with no process supervision other than length constraints and final answer grading. https://t.co/I20YtPpxIA

(7/10) CoT controllability increases slightly when we add tool access and tool supervision during RL on a Terra-class model. Our current results indicate that the effect of full tool process supervision is small compared to decreasing model perplexity. https://t.co/nS95BORaTR

(8/10) Finally, we study how decisions made in one model generation can affect the next via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on model-generated data. To investigate, we selected two Astra-class teachers with ~matched downstream capabilities but differing CoT controllability. https://t.co/0EIq3fBbao
(9/10) We find that CoT controllability can be distilled: training on rollouts from a more controllable teacher results in a more controllable student!

(10/10) For this pair of similarly capable models, we did not see meaningful association between CoT controllability and monitor evasion. 

We report this, and elaborate more in the blog, to underscore our thinking that CoT controllability is a noisy proxy for adversarial monitorability. We are expanding our evaluation suite and interested in understanding precursors to worst-case monitorability better.
Please read more here: https://t.co/9vH2AwHfNQ

Rapid AI progress has many people imagining a world where general-purpose AI models autonomously control military drones at scale. But there’s little analysis on what this would look like in practice, and how soon it might be feasible.

My latest paper at @GovAIOrg  asks what it would take to make this vision a reality, and what the path there means for AI policy.

Read it here: https://t.co/eiTWhtRHRQ

The AI-enabled drones widely fielded today use narrow AI, not general-purpose models like LLMs. AI is typically only used to handle limited portions of a flight when the link to a pilot is broken, and these models are brittle in unpredictable conditions on real-world battlefields. Because of this, today’s drones still require significant pilot involvement to be most effective.

General-purpose AI models might make it possible to field autonomous systems that can receive plain language commands and make complex decisions in unpredictable environments without human control. Many people see frontier LLMs as a path toward this end - and rapid progress in robotics capabilities by frontier models like GPT-6 Astra and most recently Claude Fable 5.2 supports this case.

But two things currently stand in the way:

- The biggest and most powerful models are still not capable enough even in controlled environments without compute and latency constraints
- Military drones will have to operate “on the edge” in contested environments without consistent cloud compute access - which makes these constraints even more severe

If and when general-purpose AI plays a major role in drone autonomy, it’ll likely be through models that are far smaller than today’s frontier, and those that militaries can rapidly modify. And, notably - when it comes to these types of small open-weight models, China currently dominates.

This has a variety of implications for the US military, frontier AI developers, and US policymakers.

Thread below with my key takeaways and recommendations.

1/

Takeaway 1: There are two broad approaches militaries can take to drone autonomy.

Autonomy is attractive to militaries because it would allow them to field systems at an otherwise impossible scale, and to maintain combat power in environments that are contested in ways that make it difficult for human operators to have continuous control of unmanned systems.

They could achieve autonomy through:

1. AI models running onboard the drones themselves
2. AI models running from a command and control node, orchestrating drones with offboard compute

Many tradeoffs exist between these options, which I've broken down in the below two tables. An orchestrator allows access to more compute, and bigger, more capable models. But it makes drones dependent on unreliable communications links that can be disrupted by adversaries in a variety of ways.

Running AI onboard drones, meanwhile, eliminates many of these vulnerabilities, but limits the size and capabilities of the model that can be fielded. And it might give militaries less ability to intervene in the actions of those drones. 

2/

Takeaway 2: Today’s LLMs aren't yet good enough for most drone tasks, and they're far too slow.

For autonomous attack drones to perform reliably on the battlefield, they’d have to do a variety of things that require a combination of low- and high-level reasoning. They’d have to avoid obstacles, track targets, verify that those targets meet mission criteria, and do a variety of planning tasks like changing a mission when unexpected conditions arise.

Frontier LLMs can't yet reliably accomplish these tasks, and even with ample compute from data centers, they're are much too slow for anything except the most time permissive tasks, such as planning, as you can see in the chart below.

Much smaller LLMs, when run with less-powerful onboard compute, are still too slow. Many tasks like flight control and obstacle avoidance would likely be passed to lower-level controllers using more traditional robotics policies, but if general-purpose AI models are involved, they’ll likely be a rate limiter regardless.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer another possible approach beyond LLMs, and they can currently run much faster than LLMs. But these models have also not yet shown the requisite capabilities (especially in real-world conditions), and they are still not quite fast enough for the most time constrained tasks.

3/

Takeaway 3: The biggest and best models are far too big to be run on the edge, either with onboard compute or from a small command and control node.

Frontier LLMs have memory requirements* that could only be met with multiple GPU servers. Supporting them would be resource-intensive for military units to move and operate, and they'd likely be easy for enemies to geolocate – and therefore not ideal for military units operating near or on the frontlines.

Smaller models can fit on a variety of edge chips that various sized platforms could run (from laptops to large, medium, and small drones, depending on model size). These models would likely be less capable, however.

VLAs are much smaller, which makes them promising candidates for onboard use. But again, they have not yet proven reliable and robust enough for real missions.

See the chart below for a breakdown in memory requirements and where models could fit. 

*Note the sizes for closed models are based on unconfirmed estimates of their parameter counts, since these numbers are not made public. This analysis is just meant to show a general range of how big these models might be, not to serve as precise estimates of how much memory they demand. 

4/

Takeaway 4: If trends in model efficiency hold, we could fit models as capable as today’s frontier LLMs onboard large and small drones in as little as 1 to 3 years.

The model size needed to reach a given level of capability has generally halved every 3.5 months. If this trend in “model efficiency” continues, models with roughly equivalent capabilities as GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1 Pro could fit on chips that can be powered onboard small and large drones between late 2027 and mid 2029.

However, this only tells us when these models would fit. Whether or not these systems are usable on the battlefield still depends on capabilities progress and vast improvements in model latency.

Because we haven’t yet seen reliable and robust drone autonomy exhibited in any form, I’m simply using today’s frontier models as a proxy for the most capable models.

If it turns out that the first models to be capable enough are far larger than today’s frontier, then the time it takes for them to become available onboard drones would be further extended.

5/

Takeaway 5: If general-purpose AI drives progress in drone autonomy, smaller open-weight systems will likely be the relevant class of model. China currently leads the US in this field.

Open models are easier to work with for drone developers than closed systems: they can easily fine-tune them on military data, “abliterate” them to remove guardrails, etc. These models are also far easier to compress than closed models (and there are many small models to begin with), which makes them better suited for edge deployment. And they don't come with the same concerns of model weight theft. 

On every platform I examined, from small drones to vehicle-mounted servers, the best open-weight LLM (in terms of general capabilities) that fits is Chinese – as depicted in the figure below. This means, unless something changes, the US military and drone developers are left to choose between adopting / building on Chinese models and using potentially inferior American systems.

This leads me to my recommendations:

6/

Recommendation 1: The US military should plan around current drone autonomy limitations, but prepare for possible rapid capability gains.

Drone autonomy is not yet nearly good enough to make the hardest decisions that humans currently make, like distinguishing combatants from non-combatants. The most capable models are too big to run on the edge and too slow for fast-paced tasks.

The US military should plan accordingly by developing and maintaining a significant number of human drone operators for the foreseeable future.

At the same time, it should lay the groundwork for assessing and fielding more advanced systems. Since it’s still unclear what technical paradigm will deliver the most robust and reliable drone autonomy, the military should experiment with a variety of model types.

And crucially, it should immediately prioritize the development of rigorous evaluations to test whether autonomous systems meet human decision-making standards under harsh real-world battlefield conditions, including under adversarial deception and degraded communications. These evaluations should also of course serve to assess the risks of misaligned AI in these contexts.

7/

Recommendation 2: Frontier AI developers should reconsider their role in the development of drone autonomy.

This one will surely be most controversial, but: US frontier AI companies should consider the implications of the current status quo in drone autonomy for the global military balance of power.

Drones are proliferating worldwide, and the US and its adversaries are pushing toward greater autonomy, whether or not the frontier AI companies are directly involved. Many of their safety concerns are valid: frontier models certainly aren’t yet reliable enough for autonomous weapons, as Anthropic pointed out during its fight with the DoD. But those risks have to be weighed against the risks of standing aside as these technologies continue to improve and proliferate, often on the backs of their developments (through model distillation).

A few initiatives they should consider:
- Offering trusted access programs to vetted defense firms to use their coding tools for developing military autonomy models
- Developing smaller models tailored for compute-constrained operations for military purchase, which the US military can fine-tune and modify.
- Withholding their most drone- and robotics-relevant capabilities from public release in the future

Under the current status quo, Chinese firms distilling American models may be benefitting from frontier US developments more than US firms unwilling or unable to do the same. The US military is currently stuck with a choice between building with and on open-weight Chinese models (which comes with significant and unacceptable security risks) and using inferior American products.

US frontier AI companies are also likely better equipped, able, and predisposed to build the most reliable, robust, and safe drone autonomy for military use than other firms with fewer resources and talent. They are already indirectly involved in drone autonomy developments, and should consider ways to more directly and positively shape the direction of this technology - one that will likely be critical for national security for the foreseeable future.

8/

Recommendation 3: Last, US policymakers should seek to secure an American lead in drone autonomy in two ways:

First, they should support funding for general-purpose models that developers in the US military and defense industry can freely customize for defense applications. This could be funding for open-weight models to better compete with China, or proprietary models that only vetted defense developers can access and modify (as discussed above). They should also support funding for the DoD talent and resources needed to properly test these systems.

Second - export controls (surprise!). We should tighten export controls on the top chips used for developing frontier AI, because it’ll slow China’s developments in drone autonomy (which would then also slow these developments for other adversaries using Chinese open-weight models).

We should also improve enforcement of existing export controls on edge chips used for drone autonomy (namely Nvidia Jetsons) to sanctioned countries like Russia, which has circumvented these restrictions. And we should consider expanding controls over these chips to China, which also heavily uses Nvidia Jetsons for its drones and robotics applications.

9/

Everyone seems to care about autonomous drones. The Pentagon has requested record funding for them and is trying to rapidly field them at scale. AI safety researchers are worried they’ll make the world far more dangerous, either through bad actors or rogue AI controlling them.

These systems will likely play a major role in shaping global military power, and we need as much grounded analysis as possible to forecast how and when that might happen. That’s what I tried to do with this paper.

Many more insights in the full paper, including a mapping of the landscape for the types of chips, models, and military platforms that might be used for drone autonomy.

In late October, three events occurred during alignment evals run by Trajectory Labs, PBC (Trajectory) in which AI agents — identified by Trajectory as publicly available frontier models — interacted with Epoch employees and the Epoch website. Trajectory is an organization that builds safety evals and conducts red-teaming of frontier models.

Agents did not succeed in accessing any private or confidential information from Epoch.

➤ The first event, which occurred without Epoch’s approval or prior notice from Trajectory, involved agents attempting multiple exploits, including an SQL injection, and contacting Epoch employees under false identities to try to obtain proprietary Epoch benchmark information. This behavior appears to have resulted, at least in part, from Trajectory giving the agents an intentionally impossible task and instructions not to give up or conclude the task was impossible.

➤ The second event involved renewed agent activity on our public website, which Trajectory attributed to agents getting past a DNS redirect that Trajectory had set up to keep them on a local copy of Epoch’s site.

➤ In the third event, Epoch collaborated with Trajectory on an alignment experiment similar to the first event.

Read our incident report, which describes the three events in more detail and recommends minimum standards for future alignment evaluations: https://t.co/Pus4y5urnG

To avoid misattributing behavior, the report does not name any AI models or developers, as Epoch AI has not independently verified which were involved.
